# 03.1 Embedding Images

Images bring a web page to life. An image element, written as `<img>`, places a picture directly into your page. Unlike paragraphs and headings, the `<img>` element is **self-closing** — it does not need a closing tag `</img>`. Instead, it uses two essential attributes: `src` and `alt`.

## The src Attribute: Where the Image Lives

The `src` attribute tells the browser the location of the image file. This can be a full URL (like `https://picsum.photos/400/300`) or a relative path to a file on your website. Without `src`, the browser has no image to show — you get a broken icon.

```html
<img src="https://picsum.photos/400/300">
```

This line tells the browser: "fetch the image from this URL and display it." That is all you need for a basic image — but there is one more attribute that makes your image complete.

## The alt Attribute: A Text Backup

The `alt` attribute provides a textual description of the image. It serves two important purposes:

- **Accessibility:** Screen readers read the `alt` text aloud so visually impaired users know what the image shows.
- **Fallback:** If the image fails to load (broken link, slow network), the browser displays the `alt` text instead of a broken icon.

Think of `alt` as a label on a picture frame. When the picture is missing, the label tells you what should be there. Always include `alt` — it is a best practice and required by many standards.

```html
<img src="https://picsum.photos/400/300" alt="A random landscape photo">
```

Now the image is fully described. If the URL works, you see the photo. If it fails, you read "A random landscape photo".

## Placing an Image Inside a Page

Because `<img>` is self-closing, you do not add a closing tag. The entire element is a single tag with attributes. It can live inside any block-level element, like a paragraph or a `<div>`, or directly inside the `<body>`.

The `<img>` element belongs to a group of elements called void elements. They cannot have any content inside them, so they never get a closing tag. This is different from the `<a>` element you learned earlier, which wraps around text and requires a closing tag.

You can use a local image file by setting `src` to a relative path, like `src="cat.jpg"` if the image is in the same folder as your HTML file.

Here is a minimal HTML document with an image:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>My Image Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <img src="https://picsum.photos/400/300" alt="A random landscape photo">
  </body>
</html>
```

Notice that the `<img>` tag stands alone — no `</img>` needed. This is the same pattern as the `<br>` element you saw earlier.

Now it is your turn to write an image element from scratch.

```code_challenge_proposal
In this exercise, you need to create a file called index.html with a complete HTML document. Inside the <body> element, add an <img> tag that displays an image from the URL 'https://picsum.photos/400/300' with the alt text 'A random landscape photo'. Make sure to include the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration and the <html>, <head>, and <body> elements. The image should be the only visible content on the page.
```
